sourceNotes: The forecast tier is empty this month. The positions, the open work orders, the open sales orders and the build rates were all pulled live from NetSuite on 7 October. The FILM tab of Forecasting 2026 USE ME was not, so every film shows nothing in the forecast column — not because the plan is small, but because it is not in this snapshot. Where a film has orders, the worst case still binds on orders or on the build rate, so the dates hold. A film running on the plan alone would be understated, and none currently is.

Film for each sales order is converted at the rate that film's own open work orders imply — film drawn divided by units built, observed this month. Five open sales orders convert to nothing because the product carries no film line at all: Agave Syrup, Gochujang 14g, Hot Sauce 1oz, Peanut Butter 1.15oz and Woeber's WG Mustard are all built at THEM with film bundled into tolling.

notes.title: BA Repeat is the biggest single handover
body: 1087 carries seven Misfits products and hands the lot to the blank 1094 when it runs dry. The date moves with every pull, so it is not written here — open 1094 in the table to see what it inherits and when.
The rate behind it is the Misfits projection of 13 October, not a trailing build rate. Their volume rises through the window, so the exit rate carries forward rather than the average.

notes.title: 5 plates need renewing, 2 deliberately do not
body: Due now: TJS Honey .5oz, HF Plum, Crait Repeat and Jamaican Jerk read expired; GE Thai-Ger lapsed 22 October. HF Plum is the live one — it is in the order list, so that order carries a renewal.
No renewal needed: BA Repeat and BA Chipotle. Both films are being run out, so nothing will be printed from either again. The only thing on this page that says do not spend.
Orange Marmalade has a plate and no film — those builds draw the blank now. No plate prices are held anywhere here.

notes.title: How much blank film we get through
body: Ours, at FFW: 244k m drawn in the year — about 4,690 m a week across the line. That is 1094 and 1129 together, which is the only figure worth reading: either one alone understates the draw, because the backup covers the weeks the primary sits empty.

THEM’s blank is theirs. It is inside the tolling rate, on no bill of materials and carrying no film line, so there is no quantity of it anywhere in our records and none is guessed at here. The Inventory tab lists what was built on it in units instead.

Two of those products — both Dijon mustards — only switched across this month, so nearly all of their year ran on 929 and is already counted there. Their units and our metres do not add up to a year of blank, and are not meant to.

notes.title: The backup is empty, so there is nothing behind 1094
body: 1129 is down to 1,643 m from 14,179 a month ago, with 23,935 m on open work orders against it. It runs dry on 8 October and its own order-by date passed on 10 September.

It is still relief rather than supply — 1094 is the default on a 16-week lead, 1129 reorders in four — but the relief has been doing most of the work. Over the last thirteen weeks the line drew 5,075 m a week through 1129 and only 2,018 through 1094. That is the reverse of the intended pattern, and it is why 1094's stock looks healthier per week than the line is.
With the backup at zero, a late 1094 order has nothing to fall back on. The four-week lead on 1129 is the only cushion left, and using it means ordering now.

notes.title: Everything coming still lands on the same blank
body: BA Repeat (1087) holds 115,117 m and is consumed at 2,871 m a week, so it hands 2,871 m a week to the blank on 14 July 2027 — a week later than last month's reading, because it drew less than planned. The page carries that as a step on 1094's runway.
It does not move this order. 1094's stock is gone by 1 February 2027 and the order placed now covers to roughly June, both before the step. It is the order after this one that has to be bigger.
The TJS moves to FFW would add more again. That handover is still not in the dates: the pooled TJS Honey stock is held per each and the blank per metre, and no conversion for it has been given.

notes.title: Why a film being retired never shows as short
body: We are not reordering BA Repeat 75mm, BA Repeat Lamick, BA Chipotle 9g or the TJS printed family. So a shortfall against them is not a purchasing problem — demand beyond the stock in hand transfers to the successor rather than needing an order here. Those rows read Winding down and show where the excess goes.

BA Repeat Foil has left the page entirely. We are never ordering it again: THEM run their own inventory for Ketchup and the Peanut Butter Spread and move those to a blank, so there is nothing on it for us to decide. Its 6.87M mm of backorder was theirs to clear, not ours.

notes.title: Printed stock is a runway, not a write-off
body: With TJS moving to FFW, the printed film already in hand covers the transition rather than stranding:
1095 TJS Honey per metre, already at FFW — 116,460 m, about 2.28M units, roughly 18 months at plan volume
1092 Strawberry Jalapeno at THEM — 18,999 m, about 286k units against 50,600 on order
1090 Blueberry Bourbon at THEM — 10,218 m, about 154k units, but FG 410 has already moved to white
1095 came from unit conversion IA177 in November 2025 and moved to FFW on transfer IT105 in May 2026, which is why no purchase order sits behind it. The first check is whether FFW can run these webs.

notes.title: 5 films that no bill of materials points at
body: Stock sitting against items nothing will consume until a revision is repointed: 1152 Hillside Jamaican Jerk 1.5oz — per metre, 1092 TJS Strawberry Jalapeno, 1089 Lamick Crait Repeat, 1093 3C VMet12 MP Repeat, 1131 Lamick Silver.

1152 is the only one with a decision behind it — Jamaican Jerk is moving onto it from 880, so it waits on a revision rather than an owner. The rest are conversions half-made: a metre item created or bought while the revision still points at the old twin.

notes.title: Work orders carrying no film line
body: Blank film run at THEM is theirs, inside the tolling rate — no film line, no bill of materials, and its sales orders are left out of the demand here.

A BA prefix means the film is ours, and it is the whole difference between BA Mirin .5oz (draws 929) and Mirin .5oz (THEM’s). The build refuses to write the page if a pair is ever merged. So a BA product with no film line has to say why: both mustards switched to blank, and Ketchup’s foil has run out.
Fish Sauce is a one-off — normally FFW on our blank, sent to THEM by mistake, expected back.

notes.title: Why this uses on hand rather than available
body: NetSuite's available quantity nets out what open work orders have committed. Those work orders exist to fill the same sales orders counted here, so subtracting both takes the demand off twice — on BA Repeat Foil that is 330,513 mm counted in two places.

The check that this is right: on hand plus on order minus open sales orders reproduces NetSuite's own backordered figure on HF Cherry, where 19,500 m on order against 6,686 m of shortfall on WO759 lines up exactly.

terms.def: The main chart. Each bar runs from today to the day that film runs dry, with a pin at the order-by date — the last day an order still lands in time. The vertical rule is today plus the lead time: a bar ending left of it cannot be saved by ordering now, which is what Order now means. Rows are sorted by the order you have to place soonest.
The weeks between now and the order-by date — how long you can leave it. Negative slack means the date has passed and an order placed today lands after the film has run out.

A film being run out hands its draw to its successor the week its own stock is gone, so the successor's runway shortens from that date. The date is not a guess: it is the retiring film's own stock divided by the rate it is being consumed at. BA Repeat (1087) hands 2,871 m a week to the blank on 3 July 2027, which is why an order covering mid-2027 has to be bigger than one covering this winter.
What is left over: everything on hand plus on order, minus the demand on whichever basis is selected. A minus number means the demand already exceeds the film.
How many weeks the stock lasts, at the faster of the recent build rate and the rate the selected demand basis implies over the lead time.
The day the remaining cover equals the lead time. Past it, an order placed today lands after the film has run out.

The shortfall plus one further lead time at the same rate — enough to close the gap and still be covered while the next order is in transit. For a film that is merely tight, one lead time's worth. Always check it against the supplier's roll size and minimum before sending.
On the transition timeline, the date a printed film being retired is consumed at its current draw rate.
The runout date less the lead time: the point by which the replacement blank has to be ordered and the BOM repointed.

One film held as two items — TJS Honey printed is per each at THEM (127) and per metre at FFW (1095). The page pools them into one runway, converting at the rate stated in the data, because it is one stock of one film facing one demand. Pooling is not used for the two blanks: see Default and Backup.

1094 is the default blank on a 16-week lead and carries the line's whole draw. 1129 is the backup on a 4-week lead, ordered only when 1094 will not arrive in time. They are two decisions, not one pool — but 1094 is judged at the full line rate, because every week 1129 was in the machine is a week 1094 would otherwise have supplied.

How many packs a quantity of film will run. A factor read off open sales orders already carries the 2% the bills of materials allow; one taken from the plate’s own geometry carries nothing, unless that film has its own planning buffer. The drill-down says which.
What assembly builds actually consumed over the trailing twelve months. Consumption, not a position or a forecast — it will not tie to stock on hand, and it is not meant to.

How many packs a quantity of film will run. Where the factor is the plate’s own geometry it is gross, so a 5% loss buffer comes off it; where it is observed from what builds actually drew, the waste is already in it and no buffer is applied. The drill-down says which.

The tile above the runway. It counts every film whose order-by date has already gone — an order placed today lands after the film runs out. Ours read Order now in the table; THEM's read THEM to order. Click the tile to see only those.
Film we buy whose order-by date has passed. The runway bar ends left of the lead-time rule.
The order-by date is close — the runway is less than a fifth longer than the lead time, so about three weeks of slack on a 16-week lead. One extra order or one bad yield and the date is behind you.
The runway is comfortably longer than the lead time. Nothing to do until the order-by date comes into view.

A film we have stopped reordering. It can never read short, because demand beyond the stock left transfers to its successor rather than becoming a purchase order here. The row shows how much transfers.
No work orders, no sales orders, no forecast and no recent builds on any basis. Stock is held, but nothing is drawing it — usually a film whose BOM revision still points somewhere else.
Short, but THEM stock this film, so the fix is their expedite rather than a purchase order from us.
Relief on a line, deliberately not reordered while the default is still ordering on schedule. It can read short on its own stock and still need nothing — see 1129 behind 1094.
Film on open work orders at Released or In Process. The firmest tier — production is already scheduled.
Open sales order demand with no work order raised yet, converted to film through each finished good's current BOM revision. Sold, but not yet released to the floor.
FILM tab demand beyond both of the above. Plan only — nobody has ordered it.

What the line has actually drawn, from assembly builds over the trailing weeks. On a film that is the default of a line it is the line's rate, not just what ran through that item — and it steps up on the date anything transfers in.
The largest of sales orders, forecast and the draw over the window. The default, because it is the one that does not get you caught out.
Work orders sit inside sales orders, which sit inside the forecast. A film can show all three and still be counted once — that is why the suggested order does not simply add the columns up.
Weeks from placing an order to film on the floor. 16 weeks for the Lamick blank; the backup blank 1129 reorders in 4 and is judged on its own clock whatever the box says.
Physically in the warehouse now.
On a purchase order, not yet received.
On hand but already allocated to an open work order.
A work order needs it and it is not there. A live shortage, not a forecast.

NetSuite's available quantity nets out what open work orders have committed. Those work orders exist to fill the same sales orders already counted as demand here, so subtracting both would take the same demand off twice. This page uses on hand plus on order instead.
Mighty Picnic — film we buy and own, from Lamick.
The co-packer who stocks their own film, from Maruto. Their film is shown for visibility; the orders are theirs to place.
The plant running the Lamick blank and, increasingly, the work moving off printed film.

Printed film carries the product's artwork, so it only fits one SKU. Blank (white) film is labelled afterwards and fits everything — which is why every transition on this page runs from a printed film to the same blank.

terms.term: Per metre, per mm, per each
terms.def: Each item is held in its own stock unit — metres for the newer Lamick films, millimetres for the older Maruto ones, each for per-unit items. Nothing on this page converts between them, so a plan row denominated in units against a film stocked per metre is a real error, not a rounding difference.

The bill of materials version a finished good is built to. It is what decides which film a sales order actually draws — which is why a film with stock but no revision pointing at it shows as having no demand.
The printing plate the supplier holds for a film. It lapses on a date rather than with use, and renewing it is a charge. Blanks have none, because nothing is printed on them.
The film’s next order-by date falls inside the plate’s life, so that order carries no renewal.
The plate expires before the film’s own order-by date, so the next order carries a renewal.
The plate expires within the next eight weeks — close enough that the charge lands whatever the ordering does.
Every item the plate covers is being run out, so nothing will be printed from it again and letting it lapse costs nothing. A plate still counts as needed if any item it covers is live.
